title: Rates: Counting Per Person
objective: After this level you can explain why comparing totals between a big place and a small one misleads, and why rates per person fix it.
summary: Totals mislead when places differ in size. A rate divides the count by the population, often per 100,000 people: a city with ten times the cases can have a tenth of the rate.

cards.headline: Big cities have more of almost everything. That alone tells you little.
cards.body: More people means more births, more bakeries and more broken legs. So when a big city beats a small town in some total, the first question is whether it simply has more people. Totals can't answer that.

cards.headline: Totals can't compare different sizes
cards.body: Picture a town of 10,000 people with 50 cases of flu, and a city of 1,000,000 people with 500 cases. The city has ten times as many cases. Sounds worse. But a total ignores how many people could have caught it. Counts don't take a population's size into account, so on their own they can't fairly compare places of different sizes.

cards.headline: Divide by the people
cards.body: A rate fixes that: divide the count by the population, then scale it to a round number of people. Health statisticians often use "per 100,000". The town: 50 cases among 10,000 people is 500 per 100,000. The city: 500 among 1,000,000 is just 50 per 100,000. The town's rate is ten times the city's. The comparison flipped.

cards.fact: A percent is a rate's little cousin.
cards.context: A percent is a rate per 100. Per 100,000 is the same idea with a bigger crowd, handy when events are rare. Either way, a rate answers the question a total can't: how common is this, person for person?

cards.headline: Rates: per person
learned: A percent is a rate per 100

questions.prompt: To turn a count into a rate, you divide it by _____.

options.label: the number of years
options.rationale: A rate here divides by the population, the number of people.

options.label: the biggest count you can find
options.rationale: Each place is divided by its own population.

options.label: 100,000 cases
options.rationale: Per 100,000 means per 100,000 people, after dividing by the population.

questions.explanation: A rate divides the count by the population, often scaled to per 100,000 people.

questions.prompt: The city had ten times the town's flu cases, yet only a tenth of its rate. How?

options.label: The city counted its cases wrongly
options.rationale: Both counts are fine; the populations differ.

options.label: Rates ignore big cities
options.rationale: Rates include everyone; they divide by each population.

options.label: The city had 100 times as many people
The town had more cases than the city
options.rationale: The town had 50 cases, the city 500.

questions.explanation: The city had 1,000,000 people to the town's 10,000: 100 times as many. Ten times the cases spread over 100 times the people is a tenth of the rate.

questions.prompt: Why is a percent, from Level 2, a kind of rate?

options.label: It counts per 100, as a rate can count per 100,000
It only works for money
options.rationale: Percents work for any share, not just money.

options.label: It always uses the whole population of a country
options.rationale: A percent is out of 100 of anything.

options.label: It is a total, not a share
options.rationale: A percent is a share: out of every 100.

questions.explanation: A percent is a part out of every 100: a rate per 100. Per 100,000 is the same idea with a bigger crowd.
